items.text: AMEND AND RECOMMIT TO CONSUMER PROTECTION
COMMITTEE DISCHARGED AND COMMITTED TO RULES

items.actClause: AN ACT to amend the general business law, in relation to rebate disclosures
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:  S7609

 TITLE OF BILL :

An act to amend the general business law, in relation to rebate
disclosures


 PURPOSE OF THE BILL :

This bill would require any entity offering a rebate to conspicuously
disclose to the consumer what form the rebate will be issued in, if
not in cash or check, and if any additional fees related to the
exercise or non-exercise of the rebate may apply.

 SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS :

Section 1 of the bill would amend General Business Law (GBL) § 391-p
to add new paragraphs (3)(a) and (b) to require any entity that offers
a consumer rebate to conspicuously disclose to the consumer (i) if the
rebate will be issued to the consumer in a form other than cash or a
check, such as credit, credit towards a future purchase, gift
certificate, gift card, general use prepaid card or any other form of
compensation, and (ii) if any additional fees related to the exercise
or the non-exercise of the rebate may apply.

Section 1 would also require that, any retailer advertising a rebate
clearly disclose if the rebate will be issued to the consumer in a
form other than cash or a check, such as credit, credit towards a
future purchase, gift certificate, gift card, general use prepaid card
or any other form of compensation.

Section 1 would also amend GBL § 391-p (4) of (GBL) by eliminating the
word "check," to clarify that the rebate may take any form the entity
offering the rebate deems appropriate.

Section 2 of the bill would provide for an effective date on the next
January 1 after enactment.

 EXISTING LAW :

GBL § 391-p outlines New York State law which does not provide
governing rebates.

 LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :

This is new bill.

 STATEMENT IN SUPPORT :

In recent years, rebate offers have become an increasingly popular
method of attracting consumers into retail establishments and induce
business. Consumers appreciate the opportunity to save money on items
they wish to purchase, and tend to respond favorably when rebates are
offered on such products.

Unfortunately, the manufacturer or retailer offering the rebate does
not always make the terms of the rebate clear to the consumer at the
point of sale. A national retailer recently advertised a $30 rebate
for cookware. The purchaser assumed the rebate would be in the form of
a check.  However, after consumers remitted and received the rebate,
they learned that it was provided in the form of a credit of $30
towards another purchase of a product from that manufacturer.
Additionally, when a rebate is provided for in the form of a pre-paid
card, the consumer could face undisclosed fees for activation,

checking of balances, and account maintenance for periods of
inactivity.

Accordingly, there is a need for greater disclosures in the rebate
advertisement and promotion process to enable the consumer to
determine if the deal is right for her or him. Since rebates are a
useful marketing tool for manufacturers and retailers, and can provide
consumers with great savings, it is important that this discount
mechanism remain a vital part of the marketplace for both businesses
and consumers, without being used for misleading purposes

The proposed legislation seeks to provide consumers with pertinent
information to assist in their budgeting and purchasing decisions
before any purchase is made. Consumers have a right to know if the
$150 rebate on the washing machine they are purchasing, for example,
will be remitted to them in the form of cash or check, or if they will
receive a prepaid card, subject to additional fees, for future use in
the retail outlet where they purchased the appliance.

Consumers need all internal information available to them when making
decisions that affect their wallet, in order to weather the present
economic difficulties and spend wisely for their households.

 BUDGET IMPLICATIONS :

There is no fiscal impact.

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
The Act would take effect on the first of January next succeeding the
date on which it shall have become a law.
